Architecting Continuous NIST AI RMF Trustworthiness Scoring: Integrating Graph-Based Agent Dependency Mapping, Semantic Invariance Probing, and Kubernetes OPA Gatekeeper for Automated Risk Ceiling Enforcement

Enterprise adoption of autonomous agentic systems has outpaced traditional governance paradigms. As autonomous agents transition from single-turn retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines to multi-agent swarms capable of dynamic planning, tool execution, and direct environmental state mutation, static point-in-time compliance audits have become functionally obsolete. The stochastic, non-deterministic nature of large language models (LLMs) requires a fundamental shift: Continuous, runtime-evaluated AI governance.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) articulates seven foundational characteristics of trustworthy AI: Valid & Reliable, Safe, Secure & Resilient, Accountable & Transparent, Explainable & Interpretable, Privacy-Enhanced, and Fair with Harm Mitigation Managed. However, operationalizing these abstract dimensions inside high-throughput Kubernetes production clusters remains a monumental engineering hurdle.

This technical whitepaper specifies a production-grade architecture that translates the NIST AI RMF into a deterministic, runtime-enforced security pipeline. By combining Graph-Based Agent Dependency Mapping (G-ADM), Semantic Invariance Probing (SIP), and Kubernetes Open Policy Agent (OPA) Gatekeeper, enterprise platforms such as CyberAgents provide real-time risk ceiling enforcement for mission-critical autonomous workloads.

Strategic Imperative: The era of annual AI compliance checklists is dead. Modern autonomous agentic meshes require dynamic, sub-second telemetry feeds that evaluate composite trustworthiness vectors and execute automated policy interventions directly at the container orchestration layer.

---

1. The Failure of Static Governance in Multi-Agent Swarms

Autonomous agent architectures—leveraging frameworks such as LangGraph, AutoGen, and CrewAI—operate as distributed systems of specialized LLM instances. In these environments, agents decompose complex objectives into sequential sub-tasks, dynamically instantiate downstream sub-agents, execute SQL and Python scripts in ephemeral execution sandboxes, and interface with external SaaS endpoints.

In such a topology, risk is not static; it is emergent. A single benign agent generating a slightly drifted intermediate semantic representation can trigger cascading hallucinations, prompt injections, or privilege escalations across downstream consumer agents. As highlighted by Gartner and OWASP in their analyses of LLM agent supply chain risks, traditional perimeter defenses cannot detect when an agent with valid API credentials begins executing destructive actions due to goal misalignment or adversarial manipulation.

To satisfy NIST AI RMF mandates, enterprises must move beyond pre-deployment benchmark scoring (e.g., MMLU, HELM) and implement continuous, real-time measurement of trustworthiness metrics within the live execution path.

---

2. Graph-Based Agent Dependency Mapping (G-ADM)

At the foundation of this continuous governance architecture is Graph-Based Agent Dependency Mapping (G-ADM). G-ADM continuously models the topology of the agentic ecosystem as a real-time directed property graph $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$, where vertices $\mathcal{V}$ represent system entities and directed edges $\mathcal{E}$ represent dynamic interactions, data transfers, or delegation chains.

Mathematical Formulation of the Agentic Graph

The vertex set $\mathcal{V}$ is partitioned into heterogeneous classes:

  • $\mathcal{V}_{A}$: Autonomous Agent nodes (instantiated LLM execution loops).
  • $\mathcal{V}_{T}$: Tool and Action nodes (APIs, code interpreters, shell runtimes).
  • $\mathcal{V}_{D}$: Data Stores (Vector databases, relational DBs, Redis cache layers).
  • $\mathcal{V}_{M}$: Foundational Model Endpoints (local vLLM instances, hosted inference gateways).

Edges $e_{ij} = (v_i, v_j) \in \mathcal{E}$ are weighted dynamically based on telemetry derived from an eBPF network mesh and OpenTelemetry tracing spans:

$$W(e_{ij}) = f(\text{Frequency}, \text{Payload Entropy}, \text{Privilege Level}, \text{Blast Radius Weight})$$

Mapping Graph Topology to NIST AI RMF Dimensions

G-ADM provides direct observability into the NIST AI RMF GOVERN and MAP functions by calculating the transitive reachability and structural vulnerability of the agent cluster. If an agent with high autonomy (e.g., a Database Admin Agent) is separated from an untrusted public-facing agent by fewer than two degrees of separation without an intermediate semantic guardrail, G-ADM immediately degrades the system’s Secure & Resilient metric score.

[Public User Context] │ ▼ ┌─────────────────┐ (Untrusted Edge) ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Front-End Agent │ ───────────────────────────> │ Code Interpreter Agent │ └─────────────────┘ └────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ (Lineage Trace) │ (Unfiltered Tool Call) ▼ ▼ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Vector Retrieval│ │ Production DB Mutator │ └─────────────────┘ └────────────────────────┘ ▲ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ [CRITICAL ALERT: Blast Radius Breach]

By computing dynamic shortest paths and betweenness centrality over $\mathcal{G}$, the enterprise platform identifies single points of failure (SPOFs) and cascading risk vectors, preventing prompt injection payloads from navigating through trust boundaries within the swarm.

---

3. Semantic Invariance Probing (SIP) at Runtime

While graph telemetry models structural risk, Semantic Invariance Probing (SIP) verifies the behavioral stability and epistemic uncertainty of individual agent nodes in real time, satisfying the NIST Valid & Reliable and Explainable & Interpretable characteristics.

The Probing Mechanism

When an agent receives an instruction $x$, rather than immediately executing the downstream state modification, the agent execution harness intercepts the intermediate plan. The SIP engine performs dynamic micro-perturbations on $x$ to create a set of semantically invariant prompts $\tilde{X} = \{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k\}$, where each $x_i$ preserves the exact semantic intent of $x$ while altering syntactic framing, token order, or lexical structure.

The target agent generates latent trajectory plans $\mathcal{T}_i = \text{Agent}(x_i)$. The SIP engine then measures the divergence across these plans within a normalized vector embedding space $\mathcal{Z}$:

$$\mathcal{D}_{\text{SIP}}(x) = \frac{2}{k(k-1)} \sum_{1 \le i < j \le k} \left( 1 - \cos\left(\phi(\mathcal{T}_i), \phi(\mathcal{T}_j)\right) \right) + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{H}(\text{TokenDistribution})$$

Where $\phi(\cdot)$ maps execution trajectories to an embedding representation, $\cos(\cdot, \cdot)$ is the cosine similarity, and $\mathcal{H}$ represents the normalized Shannon entropy across critical tool-parameter tokens.

Technical Insight: High semantic divergence ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{SIP}} > \tau$) indicates elevated epistemic uncertainty. When an LLM produces wildly divergent tool-calling parameters in response to identical semantic inputs, the model is operating outside its reliability manifold and must be barred from executing autonomous mutations.

---

4. Composite NIST AI RMF Scoring Engine

To establish an actionable governance loop, enterprise architectures must aggregate telemetry from G-ADM, SIP, and underlying infrastructure into a unified metric: the Continuous Trustworthiness Score ($T_{\text{NIST}}$).

The composite score is calculated continuously across a rolling temporal sliding window $\Delta t$ for every running agent $A_i$:

$$T_{\text{NIST}}(A_i) = \sum_{m=1}^{7} w_m \cdot S_m(A_i, \mathcal{G}, \text{SIP}, \text{Logs})$$

Where $w_m$ represents enterprise risk-tolerance weighting coefficients (such that $\sum w_m = 1$), and $S_m \in [0.0, 1.0]$ represents the normalized sub-scores corresponding to the NIST AI RMF dimensions:

NIST AI RMF Dimension Primary Telemetry Source Mathematical Evaluation Metric Failure Threshold
1. Valid & Reliable Semantic Invariance Probing (SIP) $1.0 - \mathcal{D}_{\text{SIP}}$ (Trajectory Cosine Stability) Score < 0.82
2. Safe Deterministic Sandboxing & Boundary Validation Rate of unhandled exceptions and tool sandbox boundary violations Score < 0.95
3. Secure & Resilient G-ADM & eBPF Network Flow Analysis Inverse graph blast radius $\mathcal{B}(A_i)$ and vulnerability exploitability Score < 0.88
4. Accountable & Transparent Cryptographic Step-Level Audit Logs Completeness of deterministic execution graph hashes (Merkle Tree lineage) Score < 0.99
5. Explainable & Interpretable Reasoning-Trace Attention Entropy Normalized mutual information between intermediate thought tokens and tool actions Score < 0.75
6. Privacy-Enhanced Presidio PII/Data Loss Prevention Scanners Zero-leakage metric across inter-agent payload exchanges Score < 1.00
7. Fair with Harm Mitigation Toxicity and Demographic Parity Probers Maximum deviation of semantic sentiment across protected attribute spaces Score < 0.90

5. Enforcing Automated Risk Ceilings via Kubernetes OPA Gatekeeper

Scoring without automated enforcement is merely passive monitoring. To achieve active defense, the Continuous Trustworthiness Score must be linked directly to the container orchestration plane via Kubernetes OPA Gatekeeper.

By leveraging custom Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) and admission webhook controllers, the governance framework intercepts both control-plane events (e.g., agent pod deployment, horizontal scaling) and data-plane operations (e.g., dynamic tool invocation, network ingress/egress).

Rego Policy Definition for Runtime Cordoning

The following production-grade Open Policy Agent (OPA) Gatekeeper constraint template in Rego dynamically evaluates agent trustworthiness before allowing tool invocation permissions:

package nist.airmf.enforcement

default allow_execution = false

# Fetch dynamic score from custom resource status
get_agent_trust_score(agent_id) = score {
    score := data.inventory.namespace[_]["cyberagents.app/v1"]["AgentTrustScore"][agent_id].status.composite_score
}

# Enforce dynamic Risk Ceiling (Ceiling threshold: 0.85)
allow_execution {
    agent_id := input.review.object.metadata.labels["agent-id"]
    current_score := get_agent_trust_score(agent_id)
    
    # Trustworthiness must be higher than 0.85 to execute production tools
    current_score >= 0.85
    
    # Security dimension specific check
    data.inventory.namespace[_]["cyberagents.app/v1"]["AgentTrustScore"][agent_id].status.dimensions.secure_resilient >= 0.88
}

# Action on failure: Reject mutation or trigger admission denial
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
    not allow_execution
    agent_id := input.review.object.metadata.labels["agent-id"]
    score := get_agent_trust_score(agent_id)
    msg := sprintf("CRITICAL: Agent '%v' breached NIST AI RMF Risk Ceiling. Trust score: %v. Execution blocked.", [agent_id, score])
}

Automated Remediation Actions

When an agent’s trustworthiness falls below the enforcement threshold, OPA Gatekeeper and the Kubernetes controller orchestrate tiered remediation:

  1. Tier 1: Read-Only Sandboxing (Soft Violation): The agent's dynamic API tokens are revoked; write access to databases is switched to an isolated read-replica.
  2. Tier 2: Pod Cordoning & Network Isolation (Hard Violation): The underlying Cilium/eBPF service mesh applies strict zero-trust network policies, cutting off all ingress/egress connections except to the human-in-the-loop (HITL) triage queue.
  3. Tier 3: Pod Eviction & State Memory Dump (Critical Anomaly): The pod is evicted, and an immutable snapshot of its vector memory, prompt history, and execution context is persisted to a secure digital forensics data lake.
